propositions.text: The claimant is a 56-year-old male from El Salvador claiming refugee protection under IRPA ss. 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 56), is a male from El Salvador. He claims refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a 56-year-old male from El Salvador claiming refugee protection under IRPA ss. 96 and 97(1), court states.

propositions.text: The claimant is a XXXX XXXX by profession with a practice in XXXX XXXX XXXX in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: The claimant states that he is a XXXX XXXX by profession. He says that he resided in XXXX, El Salvador and he had a XXXX and his own practice in XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: The claimant's XXXX XXXX consisted of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and one XXXX XXXX.
propositions.quote: He states that the XXXX XXXX consisted of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and one XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a XXXX XXXX by profession with a practice in XXXX XXXX XXXX; his XXXX XXXX consisted of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and one XXXX XXXX, court states.

propositions.text: In late XXXX 2005, a man came to the claimant's XXXX 'XXXX' XXXX and spoke to him.
propositions.quote: He maintains that in late XXXX 2005, a man came to his XXXXX "XXXX" XXXX.

propositions.text: While the claimant was XXXX XXXX, a police officer and XXXX XXXX of the claimant came into the XXXX and was present.
propositions.quote: He states that while he was XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX ("XXXX"), who was a police officer and a XXXX XXXX of the claimant, came into the XXXX and was in the XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: The police officer left a few minutes after the man left the XXXX.
propositions.quote: When the XXXX left the XXXX XXXX also left a few minutes later.

propositions.text: The police officer returned the next day and told the claimant the man was wanted and a member of 'La Mara 18' gang, with XXXX XXXX just outside the XXXX.
propositions.quote: XXXX returned to the XXXX the next day and told the claimant that the XXXX was a wanted man and a member of the "La Mara 18" gang. XXXX said that he had XXXX XXXX just outside the XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: In late XXXX 2005, a man came to the claimant's XXXX; a police officer and XXXX XXXX was present and later told claimant the man was a wanted 'La Mara 18' gang member, court states.

propositions.text: After the incident, the claimant received threatening calls from 'La Mara 18' accusing him of tipping off police.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that after this incident he received numerous threatening telephone calls from the "La Mara 18" gang threatening to kill him and accusing him of "tipping off the police" regarding one of their members.

propositions.text: After the second threat, claimant went to local police who tried to trace calls but could not help without proof.
propositions.quote: He states the police tried to trace the calls but their system was unable to do so. He maintains they told him since they did not have proof that the calls happened they could not help him.

propositions.text: Next day, claimant received a call warning him to take care as he used public transport and was exposed to danger.
propositions.quote: He states that the next day he received a telephone call saying he should take care of himself since he took public transportation to work every day. He was very exposed to danger.

paragraphs.summary: After the incident, claimant received threatening calls from 'La Mara 18', went to police who could not help, and received further warnings, court states.

propositions.text: In XXXX 2004, the claimant's XXXX in their complex received similar threats from 'La Mara 18'.
propositions.quote: He alleges that in XXXX 2004, the XXXX in their complex received similar threats from "La Mara 18"

propositions.text: In the same month, the XXXX was shot and killed outside his home by 'La Mara 18' members for unknown reasons.
propositions.quote: and the same month he was shot and killed outside his home in XXXX XXXX by members of "La Mara 18". He states that the reason for the killing was unknown.

propositions.text: Claimant became fearful and went to the USA on XXXX 2005 using a multiple visa obtained in 1999.
propositions.quote: He says that he became fearful and he went to the United States of America (USA) on XXXX, 2005, using a multiple visa he obtained in 1999.

paragraphs.summary: In XXXX 2004, claimant's XXXX received threats and was killed by 'La Mara 18'; claimant fled to USA in 2005 using a multiple visa, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant hired an immigration consultant in USA who promised to help obtain permanent residence but was arrested for overstaying visa in XXXX 2006.
propositions.quote: He states that he could not afford a lawyer so he hired an immigration consultant who promised to help him obtain permanent residence in the USA. He says that the consultant told him that he would take care of everything and he should carry on with his life and even work. He maintains that on XXXX, 2006, US immigration officers picked him up and accused of overstaying his visa.

propositions.text: Claimant told officers consultant was handling matters; he was detained, sister paid $5,000 bail, and he was released with court order to leave in 120 days.
propositions.quote: He told them the consultant was looking after his immigration matters. They told him that there was nothing in their system and they arrested and detained him. He says his sister paid $5,000 US bail and he was released on condition that he appear in court on XXXX, 2007. When he appeared in court, the Judge granted him 120 days to leave the country voluntarily.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant hired a consultant in USA, was arrested for overstaying visa in 2006, detained, bailed out, and ordered to leave in 120 days, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant arrived in Canada on June 27, 2007 and claimed refugee protection the same day.
propositions.quote: He arrived in Canada on June 27, 2007 and he made a claim for refugee protection on the same day.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant arrived in Canada on June 27, 2007 and claimed refugee protection the same day, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Claimant's oral testimony and documents establish his identity as a national of El Salvador.
propositions.quote: The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documentation filed,2 establish his identity as a national of El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's testimony and documents establish his identity as a national of El Salvador, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant's statements about police involvement and threats are inconsistent between application and PIF forms.
propositions.quote: In his Application for refugee protection3 the claimant stated that the persons who telephoned him said that they belonged to "La Mara 18". He also said that he was not sure why they threatened him. He also specifically stated that he did not call the police because "they would kill me more faster." In his original Personal Information Form4 (PIF) narrative he did not mention that he had gone to the police as a result of the telephone threats. In his amendment to the PIF, he stated that he went to the police after the second telephone call and they could not trace the call.

propositions.text: Claimant could not explain differences in statements but said application form was read before signing, not after.
propositions.quote: He was asked why there was a difference between the statements in his application form, his original PIF narrative and his amended PIF. He could not offer an explanation but stated that his application form had been read back to him before he signed it but not after he signed it.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's statements about police involvement and threats are inconsistent; he could not explain differences, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted Federal Court case about Record of Examination and credibility but here statements were signed by claimant.
propositions.quote: The claimant submitted a case5 from the Federal Court stating that in the absence of a verifiable record of what was said by the applicant at his interview, the Board should not use a Record of Examination to impugn the applicant's credibility because it was a breach of due process for the RPD to accept the Record of Examination as accurate in the face of the applicant's sworn statement in the PIF.

propositions.text: Claimant did not mention police visit in original PIF; court concludes he never went to police.
propositions.quote: However, in this case the statements were in the claimant's application and signed by him. He did not mention going to the police in his original PIF. If he had gone to the police it would have been an important fact to include in his application form or his original PIF. I conclude that he never went to the police on any occasion.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's signed statements contradict police visit claim and concludes he never went to police.

propositions.text: Whether claimant has a link to any of the five Convention refugee grounds.
propositions.quote: The next issue is whether or not the claimant has a link to any of the five Convention grounds.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issue whether claimant has a link to any Convention refugee grounds.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges fear of 'La Mara 18' gang and imputed political opinion from being called a traitor.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he fears members of "La Mara18" gang. The claimant submitted that because he was allegedly called a traitor that this could be considered an imputed political opinion.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence gang is intertwined with government; government actively acts against gangs.
propositions.quote: There is no persuasive evidence that the gang is so powerful or the corruption in El Salvador is so great that the gang could be considered intertwined with the government. There is documentary evidence that the government has actively initiated actions against the gangs in El Salvador.6

propositions.text: On balance, claimant could not be imputed to express political opinion against Mara 18.
propositions.quote: I conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, it could not be imputed that the claimant was expressing a political opinion against Mara 18.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges fear of 'La Mara 18' and imputed political opinion; court finds no evidence gang is government-linked and claimant not expressing political opinion.

propositions.text: Victims of crime, corruption or vendettas generally fail to establish nexus to Convention grounds, per Federal Court cases.
propositions.quote: There are a number of Federal Court cases, which have held that victims of crime, corruption7 or vendettas8 generally fail to establish a link between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds in the definition of Convention refugee.

propositions.text: Board upheld where claimant was target of personal vendetta or victim of crime, lacking nexus to Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The Board has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of a personal vendetta9 or where the claimant was a victim of crime.10

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court cases hold victims of crime or vendettas generally fail to establish nexus to Convention grounds; Board upheld in such findings, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant's fear is not linked to race, nationality, religion, political opinion or social group; no government link.
propositions.quote: The claimant's fear in this case is not linked to race, nationality, religion, real or imputed political opinion or to membership in a particular social group. There is no evidence that there was any link to any government organization.

propositions.text: Claimant is a victim of crime or vendetta without link to Convention ground; claim under s.96 IRPA fails.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the claimant is a target as a victim of crime or vendetta, and it does not provide the claimant with a link to a Convention ground. Therefore, the claimant is not a Convention refugee and the claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails.

propositions.text: Balance of analysis proceeds under section 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The balance of the analysis in this decision is pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's fear is victim of crime or vendetta without Convention ground link; s.96 claim fails; analysis continues under s.97 IRPA.

propositions.text: Whether claimant is personally at risk of death, cruel or unusual treatment or torture on return to El Salvador, risk not faced generally by others.
propositions.quote: The next issue is whether, on the balance of probabilities, the claimant is personally at risk to his life or at risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or risk of torture, if he returns to El Salvador and the risk is not faced generally by other individuals in or from El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issue whether claimant faces personal risk of death or cruel treatment not faced generally by others if returned to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant was not subjected to danger of torture as no government involvement or complicity found.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant was not subjected to a danger of torture as there was no government involvement or complicity as required by the definition of torture.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant was not subjected to torture risk due to lack of government involvement.

propositions.text: Risk faced by claimant is general to all people in El Salvador; claimant not a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I find that the risk faced by the claimant is one that is faced generally by all people in El Salvador and therefore he is not a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's risk is general to all in El Salvador; claimant not in need of protection.

propositions.text: Section 97(1) IRPA defines person in need of protection as one facing personal risk to life or cruel treatment not faced generally by others in every part of country.
propositions.quote: Section 97(1) of the IRPA states: A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally,... (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if... (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (emphasis added)

paragraphs.summary: Court states s.97(1) IRPA defines person in need of protection as facing personal risk not faced generally by others in every part of country.

propositions.text: Risk under s.97(1)(b)(ii) IRPA must be personal and faced in every part of country, not generally faced by others; two concepts to consider.
propositions.quote: A reading of this section of the IRPA leads to the conclusion that the risk, in addition to having to be personal also has to be one that would be faced in every part of the country and was not generally faced by others. There are therefore two separate concepts that have to be considered in dealing with this portion of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains s.97(1)(b)(ii) IRPA risk must be personal and faced in every part of country, not generally faced by others; two concepts involved.

propositions.text: Youth gangs (maras) and violent crime are major threats to public security in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: According to a sheet published by the Bureau for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, youth gangs (maras) and a wave of violent crime that they have brought about are major threats to public security in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Gang members are ultra violent and have created a parallel world with its own rules and economy.
propositions.quote: It is reported that gang members are ultra violent and have built a parallel world with its own rules, initiation rites, economy and moral standards.

paragraphs.summary: The court states youth gangs are major threats in El Salvador and have created a parallel violent world with their own rules.

propositions.text: Gangs engage in many illegal activities including drug trafficking, carjacking, rape, and murder.
propositions.quote: The gangs engage in many illegal activities, from drug and arms trafficking to carjacking, grand larceny and trafficking in persons as well as witness tampering, rape, and murder.

propositions.text: MS-13 and Mara 18 are the two most notorious gangs in El Salvador, terrorizing the population.
propositions.quote: The MS-13 and its rival gang, the Mara 18 (MS-18) are the two most renowned maras in El Salvador, striking terror into the Salvadoran population.

paragraphs.summary: The court states gangs commit many crimes; MS-13 and Mara 18 are notorious gangs terrorizing El Salvador.

propositions.text: The claimant faces a generalized risk from MS-18 gang present throughout El Salvador.
propositions.quote: the risk faced by the claimant from the MS-18 gang would be faced in every part of the country and is faced generally by all people in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Criminal activity against the claimant is a generalized risk faced by all individuals in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: the criminal activity against him is faced generally by all individuals in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant was one of many victims and everyone in El Salvador was frightened of gangs.
propositions.quote: In his testimony, the claimant also stated that when he was in El Salvador everyone was frightened of these gangs. The claimant here was one of their many such victims.

propositions.text: Claimant's personal targeting does not remove him from the generalized risk category.
propositions.quote: The fact that the claimant may have been identified personally as a target because of suspicion that he gave information leading to the arrest of a gang member does not necessarily remove him from the generalized risk category

propositions.text: Federal Court upheld Board's finding of generalized risk for gang victims.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has upheld the Board in finding generalized risk for various victims of the gangs.

propositions.text: The claimant faces a generalized risk throughout El Salvador like all individuals from that country.
propositions.quote: The risk faced by the claimant would be faced by the claimant in every part of the country and is faced by all individuals in or from El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant faces a generalized risk from gangs throughout El Salvador, consistent with Federal Court precedent.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimant is not a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not in need of protection on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: There is adequate state protection in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: I find that there is adequate state protection in El Salvador

propositions.text: Claimant has not taken all reasonable steps to pursue available state protection.
propositions.quote: the claimant has not taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances of this case to pursue the available state protection.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: claimant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection, with clear and convincing evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adequate state protection exists and claimant failed to pursue or rebut it with clear evidence.

propositions.text: There is a presumption that states can protect citizens unless in complete breakdown.
propositions.quote: There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens.

propositions.text: Claimant must prove on balance of probabilities that state protection is inadequate.
propositions.quote: A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: Claimant can rebut presumption by clear and convincing evidence of state's inability to protect.
propositions.quote: A claimant can rebut the presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

propositions.text: Claimant may provide testimony of others or personal incidents showing state protection failure.
propositions.quote: a claimant might advance testimony of similarly-situated individuals let down by the state protection arrangement or the claimant's testimony of past personal incidents in which state protection did not materialize.

propositions.text: Claimant must approach state for protection when reasonably forthcoming.
propositions.quote: The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.

propositions.text: Adequacy, not perfect effectiveness, is the test for state protection.
propositions.quote: recent Federal Court decisions have held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than the effectiveness per se.

propositions.text: Protection need not be perfect; serious efforts by state suffice.
propositions.quote: the preponderant case-law supports the test of an 'adequate' state protection rather than an 'effective or perfect' state protection.

propositions.text: One measure is whether state is making serious efforts to protect citizens.
propositions.quote: One accepted measure of assessment is whether the state is making "serious efforts" to protect its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains legal principles on state protection presumption, burden of proof, and adequacy standard from case law.

propositions.text: No state guarantees perfect protection; less than perfect protection is insufficient to deny protection claim.
propositions.quote: no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state, in not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim

propositions.text: Effective control and serious efforts by state negate unwillingness or inability to protect.
propositions.quote: where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.

propositions.text: Less than perfect protection does not mean state is unwilling or unable to protect.
propositions.quote: Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states imperfect protection does not prove state unwillingness or inability to protect under law.

propositions.text: Burden to prove absence of state protection depends on state's democracy level.
propositions.quote: the burden to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.

propositions.text: El Salvador is a constitutional, multiparty democracy with generally free and fair elections.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence before the Board indicates that El Salvador is a constitutional, multiparty democracy. In March the voters selected Carlos Maurizio Funes Cartagena of the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) as president for a five-year term in generally free and fair elections.

propositions.text: Civilian authorities maintain effective control over security forces in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: Civilian authorities generally maintained effective control over the security forces.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds El Salvador is a democratic state with effective civilian control, affecting burden of proof on state protection.

propositions.text: National Civilian Police and Ministry of Defense maintain public and national security in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: The National Civilian Police (PNC) is responsible for maintaining public security and the Ministry of Defense for maintaining national security.

propositions.text: Military supports police but lacks arrest authority; police misconduct is investigated and sanctioned.
propositions.quote: Military personnel, however, do not have arrest authority. Through November, the PNC office of the Inspector General had received 2230 complaints of alleged police misconduct, referred 47 cases of these to special investigation units, and sanctioned 1181 officers in response to complaints filed during the year and prior years.

propositions.text: Police receive human rights training; no evidence El Salvador is in complete breakdown.
propositions.quote: most PNC officers and police academy cadets received human rights awareness training during the year. There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that El Salvador is in a state of complete breakdown.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes El Salvador's police and military roles, misconduct investigations, training, and finds no state breakdown.

propositions.text: Claimant did not go to police; if he did, only twice in short period after incident.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant did not go to the police on any occasion. If I am wrong in that finding, the claimant says that he contacted the police on two occasions.

propositions.text: Claimant left El Salvador two weeks after incident, insufficient time for police investigation.
propositions.quote: The claimant left the country on XXXX, 2005. This was only two weeks following the initial incident. This would not allow the police sufficient time to investigate the matter.

propositions.text: Claimant did not follow up with police after being told system was unavailable.
propositions.quote: claimant stated that he did not go back to the police to determine if their system was now able to trace any further telephone calls after they told him the system was unavailable after the second call.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant did not adequately pursue police protection after the incident in El Salvador.

propositions.text: El Salvador has one of the highest crime and murder rates globally.
propositions.quote: It is acknowledged that El Salvador has one of the highest crime rates and murder rates in the world.

propositions.text: There is significant gang activity in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: It is also acknowledged that there is a large amount of gang activity El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges El Salvador's high crime and gang activity levels.

propositions.text: Gang violence challenges Salvadoran law enforcement with limited resources.
propositions.quote: The gang phenomenon presents a major challenge to Salvadoran law enforcement agencies, which have limited manpower, financial resources and technical capacity.

propositions.text: Salvadoran government does not refuse assistance to gang violence victims.
propositions.quote: the Salvadoran government does not have a policy or practice of refusing assistance to persons who receive threats or are otherwise victims of gang violence.

propositions.text: US Embassy has no info of police denying assistance to gang violence complainants.
propositions.quote: the US Embassy in San Salvador has no information to suggest that persons had been denied assistance from police authorities in relation to complaints they have made relating to gang violence or threats from gang members.

propositions.text: Government prioritizes gang violence security and receives international assistance.
propositions.quote: Much of the government's current focus is on fostering and providing greater security for the public against gang violence. The Salvadoran government treats gang violence as a high priority, has expensed considerable sums to address the issue and has received technical assistance from the US and other countries to improve its law enforcement capabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Salvadoran government prioritizes gang violence and provides assistance despite resource challenges.

propositions.text: El Salvador is making serious efforts to address violence and provide adequate state protection.
propositions.quote: El Salvador is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality and police are both willing and able to protect such victims.

propositions.text: Claimant has not shown protection would be unavailable or unreasonable to seek if returned today.
propositions.quote: The claimant has not established that were he to return to El Salvador today, protection would not be reasonably forthcoming or that it is an objectively unreasonable for him to seek protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds El Salvador provides adequate protection and claimant has not shown otherwise if returned.

propositions.text: Claimant did not take all reasonable steps to pursue state protection, approaching authorities at most twice briefly.
propositions.quote: The Board finds that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances of this case to pursue the available state protection. The claimant never approached the authorities in El Salvador for help or at most, he approached them on two occasions in a short period of time.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to reasonably pursue state protection in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: The claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear evidence.

propositions.text: Considering all evidence, claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: Considering the evidence in its entirety, I find that the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection after considering all evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; claim rejected.
propositions.quote: Having considered all of the evidence, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, rejects the claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not a refugee or in need of protection and rejects the claim.
